subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is meant by 'resource security'?
options: A reliable, affordable and sustainable supply of a needed resource
Owning all of a country's mines
questions.explain: Resource security is the assured access to enough of a resource at an affordable price to meet a population's needs.

questions.q: How does climate change threaten water security?
options: It has no effect on water
It alters precipitation patterns, shrinks glaciers and increases droughts and floods
questions.explain: Warming shifts rainfall, melts the glaciers that feed rivers, and intensifies both droughts and floods, stressing water supplies.

questions.q: A major criticism of Rostow's model is that it:
options: Is Eurocentric and assumes all countries follow the same Western path
questions.explain: Critics argue the model wrongly universalises the Western experience and ignores colonial and global structural barriers.

questions.q: Which of the following is a classic 'pull factor' for migration?
options: Better job opportunities and higher wages at the destination
questions.explain: Pull factors are positive attractions of a destination, such as employment, higher wages and better services.

questions.q: The 'demographic dividend' refers to the potential economic boost when:
options: A large share of the population is of working age relative to dependants
questions.explain: A demographic dividend occurs when a country has a large working-age population relative to dependants, boosting growth potential.

questions.q: A major contemporary international migration corridor is:
questions.explain: The Mexico-to-USA corridor is one of the world's largest international migration flows, driven largely by economic factors.

questions.q: In Rostow's final stage, 'high mass consumption', the economy is dominated by what?
options: A large service sector and widespread consumer durables
questions.explain: At high mass consumption, output and employment shift to services and consumers can purchase abundant durable goods.

questions.q: What is a major sustainability concern with intensive industrial agriculture?
options: Soil degradation, water pollution from fertilisers, and high energy use
questions.explain: High-input farming can degrade soils, pollute water through nutrient run-off and depend heavily on fossil-fuel-based inputs.

questions.q: The water-food-energy nexus describes:
options: The interdependence whereby managing one resource affects the others
A trade agreement between three nations
questions.explain: The nexus highlights that water, food and energy systems are interconnected, so a decision in one affects supply in the others.

questions.q: Why are 'rare earth' and critical minerals increasingly strategically important?
options: They are essential for renewable technologies and electronics but concentrated in few countries
They are only used in jewellery
questions.explain: Critical minerals underpin batteries, magnets and electronics, yet their concentrated supply creates geopolitical vulnerability.

questions.q: How do energy TNCs act as key 'players' in the energy system?
options: They explore, extract, refine, distribute and influence prices and policy
questions.explain: Large energy TNCs dominate exploration through to distribution and wield significant influence over markets and governments.

questions.q: Internal migration is best defined as movement that:
options: Occurs within the boundaries of a single country
questions.explain: Internal migration is movement within a country, such as rural-to-urban migration, rather than across national borders.

questions.q: What is OPEC's primary role in global energy?
options: To coordinate oil production among member states to influence prices
questions.explain: OPEC is a cartel of oil-exporting nations that adjusts production quotas to influence the global price of crude oil.

questions.q: How can desalination improve water security, and what is its drawback?
options: It produces freshwater from seawater but is energy-intensive and costly
questions.explain: Desalination converts seawater to freshwater, boosting supply, but it consumes large amounts of energy and money.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'resource frontier'?
options: The expansion of resource extraction into previously inaccessible or marginal areas
A line on a price chart
questions.explain: The resource frontier is the advancing limit at which extraction reaches new, often remote or fragile, environments such as the Arctic.

questions.q: A nation's 'energy mix' refers to:
options: The blend of different energy sources used to meet demand
questions.explain: The energy mix is the combination of fossil fuels, nuclear and renewables a country uses to supply its energy.

questions.q: In Lee's migration model, 'push factors' are best described as:
options: Attractive features drawing people to a destination
Negative conditions in the origin that encourage people to leave
The personal characteristics of the migrant
questions.explain: Push factors are negative aspects of the origin area, such as unemployment or conflict, that prompt people to leave.

questions.q: Thomas Malthus argued that:
options: Food supply would always exceed population needs
Innovation would always solve resource shortages
Population would grow geometrically and outstrip food supply, which grows arithmetically
questions.explain: Malthus argued population grows geometrically while food supply grows only arithmetically, so population would outstrip food.

questions.q: What does it mean that human rights have a distinct 'geography'?
options: Protection and abuse of rights vary significantly between and within countries
Rights only apply at the equator
questions.explain: The degree to which rights are upheld differs spatially, shaped by political, cultural and economic context.

questions.q: What does reducing the 'water footprint' of agriculture aim to achieve?
options: Producing food using less water through efficient irrigation and crop choice
questions.explain: Cutting agriculture's water footprint means growing food with less water via efficient irrigation and appropriate crop selection.

questions.q: Why might unconventional gas extraction such as fracking be controversial?
options: It raises concerns over water contamination, induced seismicity and methane leakage
questions.explain: Fracking is contested due to risks of groundwater pollution, small earthquakes and fugitive greenhouse-gas emissions.

questions.q: The Social Progress Index is notable because it deliberately excludes which variable?
questions.explain: The Social Progress Index measures social and environmental outcomes without using economic indicators, complementing GDP.

questions.q: A potential social impact of large-scale immigration on a host area is:
options: An immediate fall in the host population
The disappearance of all public services
Greater cultural diversity but possible community tensions
questions.explain: Immigration can enrich host societies with diversity but may also generate social tensions over integration and resources.

questions.q: The carrying capacity of an environment is best defined as:
options: The maximum population it can support sustainably with available resources
The total land area in square kilometres
The number of migrants entering per year
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can support sustainably given its resources.

questions.q: A neo-Malthusian view of the population-resource relationship holds that:
options: Population can grow without any consequence
Resource limits will ultimately constrain population growth
questions.explain: Neo-Malthusians argue that finite resources and environmental limits will eventually check unsustainable population growth.

questions.q: Forced migration is best illustrated by:
options: A retiree moving to the coast
A graduate moving abroad for a higher salary
People fleeing a civil war as refugees
questions.explain: Forced migration involves people compelled to move by conflict, persecution or disaster, such as war refugees.

questions.q: A pro-natalist population policy is one that:
options: Encourages couples to have more children
questions.explain: Pro-natalist policies, used in some ageing-population countries, offer incentives to encourage higher birth rates.

questions.q: Why is GNI per capita (PPP) often preferred to GDP for comparing living standards between countries?
options: It adjusts for differences in the cost of living and includes income from abroad
It excludes the informal economy entirely
questions.explain: GNI counts income earned abroad, and PPP adjustment corrects for differing price levels so values are more comparable.

questions.q: What is a likely consequence of over-abstraction of groundwater from an aquifer?
options: Falling water tables, land subsidence and saltwater intrusion in coastal areas
questions.explain: Pumping water faster than recharge lowers the water table and can cause subsidence and seawater contamination near coasts.

questions.q: Which UN measure underpins the international framework for human rights?
options: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)
questions.explain: The 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights sets out the foundational global standard for human rights.
